title: The veil made of love
hookLine: Yashoda forgets the vision and goes back to simply loving her son
carry: vatsalya: loving God as your own child
tomorrow: The boy in the poisoned pool

lines: SKY, EARTH, STARS, FOR AN INSTANT.
cards: It wasn't the first time. A chapter earlier, the Bhagavata tells a smaller version. Yashoda is nursing her baby, and he yawns, the way babies do.
In that yawn, for an instant, she sees the sky, the earth, the stars, the oceans, mountains and forests. She trembles and shuts her eyes. Then the moment passes, and he's just a yawning baby again.
So what happens to the next ordinary morning, after you've seen something like that?

teach.b: Back in the yard, Yashoda is still standing over her son, bewildered, bowing inwardly to whatever this is. Then the text says something startling.

teach.h: A VEIL SHAPED LIKE A MOTHER'S LOVE.
teach.b: Krishna spreads his maya over her, his power to veil, and it takes the form of a mother's love for her son.
She forgets. The vision is gone. She sets him on her lap, her heart full of affection for him, just as before.
The story could have made her a great sage, seeing God in her child every moment. Instead the vision is taken back on purpose, and love replaces it.
King Parikshit, listening, asks the sage telling the story: what did Nanda and Yashoda ever do, to be given a love like this?
The sage answers with a former life, in which they asked for one thing: supreme devotion to the Lord, once they were born on earth. In this telling, being his parents is how that wish is granted.
So the forgetting isn't a loss. It's the gift working.

teach.h: VATSALYA: A PARENT'S LOVE FOR GOD.
teach.b: Hindus have a name for this way of loving God: vatsalya, a parent's love.
Devotional schools such as the Gaudiya and the Pushti Marg count it among the great ways to love God: not bowing to the infinite from far away, but feeding him, scolding him, holding him.

That's why, in many Hindu homes, someone wakes a small image of baby Krishna in the morning, bathes him, dresses him, offers him food before anyone else eats, and puts him to bed at night. They know what he is.
Like Yashoda, they're allowed to love who he is to them.

how: In many Hindu homes, a small image of baby Krishna, often called Laddu Gopal, is woken, bathed, dressed, fed and put to bed each day, in the spirit of Yashoda's love.

o: Krishna's power to veil, here shaped as a mother's love
the Lord's anger at being seen by human eyes
a dream Yashoda has while she is nursing the baby

p: a veil, here shaped like a mother's love
asks what Nanda and Yashoda did
loving God as a parent loves a child

s: yesterday's vision is the only time Yashoda sees the universe in him
an earlier yawn, while nursing, showed her the sky and stars for an instant.
Krishna makes Yashoda forget the vision
his maya takes the form of her love for him.
families who feed a baby Krishna image think God is only a baby
like Yashoda, they know what he is, and choose a parent's love: vatsalya.

games.q: you're Yashoda. you've just seen the whole universe inside your little boy's mouth. what happens next?
o: you bow to him and never treat him as a child again.
you forget it, and take him on your lap with love.
you run to tell the whole village.
games.why: Krishna veils the vision with a mother's love, and she forgets and holds him. Hindus call that love vatsalya, and treat it as a gift.

practice: Many Hindus offer food to God before they eat, then eat it as prasad, a gift given back. At your next meal, set a little aside before the first bite, and offer it the way Yashoda fed her boy: with love, not ceremony.
If you pray, say Krishna's name, or the name you use. Then eat it slowly. If you don't pray, offer that bite in thanks for someone who feeds you.

wordCard.voice: Maya. Krishna's power to veil, which falls over Yashoda as a mother's love, and lets her forget the vision and simply love her son again.

orig.note: Sanskrit: maya, the veiling power; here it takes the form of a mother's love.

carryVoice: Your line: vatsalya: loving God as your own child. Tomorrow, a poisoned pool in the river. Day eight hundred ninety-one, done.
